analysis.one_liner: Directs EPA to write strict limits on PFAS pollution discharged into water by nine industries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee in May 2022 and stayed there until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS ("forever chemicals") are man-made compounds used in nonstick cookware, waterproof clothing, and many industrial processes; they do not break down and can harm human health. The bill would require the EPA to set enforceable discharge limits for PFAS from nine industry categories — chemical-using manufacturers, electroplaters, textile mills, landfills, and others — by 2024-2026, publish health-based water quality criteria within three years, and require monitoring at pulp mills and airports. It died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities whose drinking water and waterways are contaminated with PFAS, including people near industrial dischargers, airports (where firefighting foam is a major PFAS source), and paper mills. The bill would force polluters to measure and limit PFAS in their wastewater rather than passing it downstream to water treatment plants and public water supplies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with PFAS in their water

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to publish human health water quality criteria for every measurable PFAS substance or class within three years of enactment [S3].

Sets deadlines for final rules limiting PFAS discharge from three waves of industries: organic chemicals/plastics, electroplating, and metal finishing by June 2024; textile mills, electronics, and landfills by June 2025; leather tanning, paint, and plastics molding by December 2026 [S3].

Immediately requires PFAS monitoring in permits for pulp, paper, and paperboard mills and airports, with a decision due by the end of 2023 on whether discharge limits are feasible for those categories [S3].
Covers discharges into publicly owned treatment works, so industrial users must account for PFAS before it reaches municipal wastewater plants that are not designed to remove it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Industries that use or discharge PFAS — chemical and plastics makers, electroplaters, metal finishers, textile mills, electronics and paint manufacturers, leather tanneries, landfills, airports, and paper mills — would face monitoring and treatment costs. Some costs could pass through to consumers as slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: the nine covered industry categories would have to install monitoring and treatment for PFAS in wastewater, and some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers through higher prices [S3].

Deadlines may be hard to meet: the bill requires the EPA to finalize effluent guidelines for multiple industries within two to four years, faster than the agency's typical rulemaking pace, raising the risk of missed deadlines or legal challenges.

The bill addresses water discharge only; it does not clean up PFAS already in soil and groundwater or restrict the chemicals' ongoing use in products, so contamination can continue through other pathways.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is real and broad: PFAS contamination of drinking water is widespread and the compounds persist indefinitely, so limits at the source are cheaper than treating water downstream. The main cost falls on the discharging industries, and the compressed deadlines are aggressive but the stakes justify speed. On balance, a well-targeted public health measure whose principal cost falls on polluting industries.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day it was introduced and then to a subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas introduced the bill on May 10, 2022, with 27 cosponsors — 26 Democrats and 1 Republican [S1, S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment; no further action appears in the record before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that discharge PFAS avoided new monitoring and treatment requirements, and water utilities and their customers continue to bear the cost of removing the chemicals downstream.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS-discharging industries, which avoided new limits

for.name: Rep. Chris Pappas
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require EPA discharge limits and health criteria for PFAS.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Peter DeFazio (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed in committee and its subcommittee for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 26 Democrats and 1 Republican cosponsored — but no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: PFAS-using manufacturers (chemicals, plastics, electroplating, metal finishing, textiles, electronics, paints, leather tanning)
industries.note: The bill would set enforceable deadlines for these industries to monitor and limit PFAS in their wastewater, imposing treatment costs. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs against the public's interest in uncontaminated water.

industries.industry: Landfills, airports, and pulp and paper mills
industries.note: These dischargers would face mandatory PFAS monitoring, with possible discharge limits for pulp mills and airports by 2027. Airports are a significant PFAS source through firefighting foam.

Because the bill covers discharges into publicly owned treatment works, industrial PFAS would be limited at the source, reducing the burden on treatment plants and drinking water systems that cannot economically remove the chemicals themselves.
